title: The Blair Witch Project
full_review:
Some enterprising rookie filmmakers have basically made something out of almost nothing with ``The Blair Witch Project'' (Artisan). With virtually no budget, the writing-directing- editing team of Eduardo Sanchez and Daniel Myrick filmed their simple idea in the outdoors, using a minimal cast to create a spooky horror film that parades as reassembled documentary footage. The premise is that three Maryland youngsters around age 19 go into a local woods to explore on video and 16mm film an old myth about a resident murderous witch.

The trio never emerged again, but a year later the footage from their five days and harrowing nights in the forest was discovered and is presented as a record of their doomed filmmaking project.

Calling the shots is the initially self-assured Heather (Heather Donahue), who insists on filming themselves on video even as they trek through the woods and anticipate an overnight stay. Laid-back cameraman Josh (Joshua Leonard) agreeable but sound man Mike (Michael Williams) is quickly annoyed when Heather falsely claims they are not lost since she has a flimsy map of the general area. Matters go from bad to worse when they hear possibly human noises during the freezing, pitch-black night and find deliberately arranged rocks and piles of tied-up twigs outside their tent in the morning.

Nor can they find their way out of the wood as their food dwindles and voodoo-like tree hangings convince them they are indeed being hunted. As passing days, hunger, cold and terror all combine to drive them nearly insane with fear and dread, they continue to record their hysterical accusations against one another for initiating the project, getting lost, and tossing the map into a creek. When one vanishes overnight, the other two finally follow his distant screams to the ruins of a house while the camera records what it can of their fate.

By in effect having the three actors shoot footage in the woods without a script, the actual filmmakers achieve a sense of immediacy with the final product. The terrified threesome do seem more and more disoriented and the urgency of their situation is palpable.

This was a kind of ``method'' filmmaking, as the cast was left pretty much on their own in the wild with little food over an eight-day shoot, and by the final scene they do appear adversely affected. And so, with no special effects or monsters jumping out of the dark, the filmmakers rely on what is imagined to conjure up horror for their movie without need for any graphic violence.

But what undermines the ominous atmosphere is their shrill screaming and cursing until four-letter words overwhelm the dialogue and make one wish for a quick ending, happy or otherwise. Their psychological deterioration could have made for compelling character studies, but the filmmakers chose a lazier course of just having them substitute profanity for profundity. With its hand-held cameras, the visuals are jittery to the point of dizzying at times, but that does add to the verisimilitude of the situation.

When Heather confesses directly to her camera near the conclusion, ``I'm scared to open my eyes and I'm scared to close them'' the audience won't doubt her for a minute. With its spare visuals and sole focus on their plight, the movie seems long at a mere 87 minutes, but it certainly is distinctive from the usual bucket-of- blood horror flick.

Because of fleeting violence, much menace, some profanity and constant rough language, the U.S. Catholic Conference classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R - - restricted.
